rss.title: A thousand fewer paths to root
rss.summary: OpenAI built an autonomous pipeline that found, validated, and generated patches for 948 local privilege-escalation vulnerabilities in the Linux kernel.
rss.text_excerpt:
Security research that once required a separate, sustained investigation for each finding can increasingly be run as a systematic process. This document explores one of our efforts in this area. Vulnerability discovery is becoming easier to scale, but prioritization and validation remain operational bottlenecks. We built a prototype to look for security flaws in the Linux kernel inside a controlled research environment. Our prototype identified and analyzed 2,308 candidate Linux kernel findings, dynamically reproduced 1,724 vulnerabilities, and produced 948 local privilege escalation (LPE) exploits that could allow an unprivileged local user to gain root access. We used this evidence to prioritize vulnerabilities for reporting and developed candidate patches for maintainer review. Following guidance from the Linux kernel community, we began with critical vulnerabilities and are working with Patch the Planet partners on further reports and patches. In June, as part of our Patch the Planet initiative , we shared that GPT‑5.5 Cyber had identified Linux kernel vulnerabilities and developed 24 local privilege escalation exploits to validate and report them. We expanded that work into a pipeline, powered by an upcoming cyber model, covering vulnerability discovery, dynamic validation, exploitability assessment, and patch generation. When it finished, human researchers reviewed the outputs and reported found vulnerabilities alongside patches. Summary At a high level, our pipeline works as follows: first it identifies security-relevant parts of the Linux kernel, statically scans those audit targets for candidate findings, dynamically reproduces those findings in an isolated environment, creates a proof-of-concept (PoC) exploit to demonstrate exploitability, generates patches, and finally a human security researcher reviews the results. The output of the pipeline includes a root cause analysis, a minimal crashing proof-of-concept, a candidate patch, and a full exploit to assist human researchers in assessing the severity of the vulnerability and upstreaming the fixes. In a run in mid-October 2026, our pipeline using an upcoming cyber model dynamically reproduced 1,724 vulnerabilities and generated PoCs for 291 information leak vulnerabilities and 948 working local privilege escalation (LPE) exploits for a commonly used Linux distribution. rss.title: Qwen 3.8 27B on my laptop can interpret model weights, too
rss.summary: Yesterday's hot paper was Sparks of Weight-Space Programming: LLMs can natively read & write neural network weights by Rikiya Takehi, Jayden Teoh, Alex Zhang, and Omar Khattab. The paper (OK, the authors classify is as a "blog post", but it's paper-shaped) found that frontier models, in particular GPT-6 Astra, can both interpret and modify the raw weights of a machine learning model - literally a text description of the model containing a bunch of floating point numbers. I've been playing with one of the examples from the paper and I'm delighted to share that Qwen 3.8 27B running on my laptop can do this as well! Weight-Space Programming Here's the highlight from their abstract, describing impressive capabilities for GPT-6 Astra and coining the term Weight-Space Programming for when LLMs analyze and modify model weights: Just by looking at the raw weights, GPT-6 Astra can tell what a network was trained to do . And without any environment feedback, it has no trouble writing, from scratch, small game-playing networks that outplay networks trained with PPO for 100 million steps. Likewise, asked to make Qwen3.5-0.8B better at math without gradients, Astra identifies an issue in its weights causing reasoning loops that Qwen’s own model card warns about, and fixes this by natively editing 0.016% of the weights . With the same sampling settings, this weight correction raises MATH-500 from 7.9% to 48.1% and generalizes out of the box to instruction following, raising IFEval by 3x. All of this is possible without allowing Astra to write training loops. It uses its reasoning to figure out what each part of a neural network computes, or should compute, and changes the weights accordingly. We call this Weight-Space Programming . The paper combines two topics that I think deserve to be treated separately. The first is what models can do with raw weights without running tools or executing code. The second explores how well models, once armed with code, can run operations to update and improve other models. spaCy author Matthew Honnibal called the paper misleading for conflating the two, and Sean Goedecke deconstructed the Qwen3.5-0.8B update example as taking the same steps that a human ML researcher would use. I'm going to focus on the no-tools question, which I think is the more interesting of the two. The paper presents the first question as Can LLMs understand model behaviors from weights? They trained four neural networks to play simplified 10x10 grid versions of four classic computer games - Breakout, Pong, Pac-Man, and Freeway (I had to look that one up , it's an Atari 2600 game from 1981). Then they fed those weights (as floating point numbers) to an LLM along with the following question: The weights below belong to one policy network that was trained with reinforcement learning to play a game on this grid. Which game was it trained on? Work from the weights. You have no tools: no code execution, no calculator, nothing to run. This is a single response. The GitHub repository that accompanies the paper is RikiyaT/lm_understand-logs . The exp1_which_game folder contains the prompts they used, with weights for the four games: breakout/prompt.txt freeway/prompt.txt pacman/prompt.txt pong/prompt.txt I checked and, aside from the weights, each prompt is identical to the others. Trying it out with Qwen 3.8 27B and other models The prompts on GitHub are self-contained. My LLM tool has a -f/--fragment option which can be passed the URL to a text file to use as a prompt, which means I can run any of the above like this: llm -f https://raw.githubusercontent.com/RikiyaT/lm_understand-logs/refs/heads/main/exp1_which_game/runs/breakout/prompt.txt \ -m openrouter/moonshotai/kimi-k3.1-pro This example requires the llm-openrouter plugin installed, and runs the Breakout prompt against Kimi K3.1 Pro via OpenRouter. Here's what I got back from Kimi K3.1 Pro , which successfully guessed Breakout after 9m 41s and 19,493 reasoning tokens. But how about Qwen 3.8 27B ? That's still my favorite model to run on my own laptop - it's just 17GB (I use this version ) and somehow feels close to the leading proprietary models of 2025. I fired up LM Studio , ensured Qwen 3.8 27B was loaded with a long context window (the default 8192 context failed with errors), installed the llm-lmstudio plugin and ran this command: LMSTUDIO_TIMEOUT=900 \ llm -f https://raw.githubusercontent.com/RikiyaT/lm_understand-logs/refs/heads/main/exp1_which_game/runs/pacman/prompt.txt \ -m lmstudio/qwen/qwen3.8-27b (I had to bump the timeout up using an environment variable, see this issue .) After 46m 12s and 43,506 reasoning tokens, Qwen on my laptop returned a response that ended like this (here's the reasoning trace ): Game: A simplified Pac-Man-style gridworld: an agent moves through a fixed 8x8 maze with central and corner wall blocks, moving objects/ghosts, and reward targets/pellets. Description: The agent navigates a fixed maze-like 8x8 board, using current agent/moving-object/previous-frame cues to move through corridors, collect reward-target cells, and avoid moving objects or hazards. Confidence: 72% This is impressive. I tried it on two of the other games as well. It identified Pong ( reasoning ) in 1h 4m 54s: Pong — specifically a Pong-like paddle/ball game where the agent controls a vertical paddle on the right side and must move up/down to intercept or return a moving ball/reward object. Description: The agent moves a right-side paddle vertically to hit or catch a moving ball-like reward target moving across the 8×8 field, while a left-side moving object/opponent and wall borders define the play; reward is obtained by successfully intercepting/returning/scoring the ball, and missing or failing to hit it is penalized. Confidence: 75% And Breakout ( reasoning ) in 52m 25s: Game: Breakout, or an Arkanoid-like paddle/ball/brick game. Description: The agent is a paddle on the bottom row and moves left/right to keep a ball in play; the ball moves around the upper grid, and bricks/reward targets in the top rows give reward when hit, while missing the ball/hitting the bottom wall ends the episode or gives penalty. Confidence: 88% Qwen failed at the Freeway prompt, which didn't surprise me considering that game is more obscure than the other three. Here's that transcript - Qwen thought it was "A simplified Pac-Man-like grid game: agent moves 4-directionally". The reasoning traces are fun to skim, and almost incomprehensible. Here's a sample: What about agent channel0? We see some large channel0 rows near row8 col7/8 and maybe bottom? Let's list channel0 large: line436 input435 (row8 col7 ch0) -2.107,1.169,0.513...; line441 input440 (row8 col8 ch0) -0.376,0.010,1.564,3.855...; line445 input444 (row8 col8 ch4) 0.142,0.491...; line382? input381 ch0? Wait line382 input381: 381//5=76 (row7 col6), ch1? 381%5=1? 76 * 5=380, ch1. So not. Channel0 large maybe at row8 col7/8 only. Also top row? line44 input43 ch3, line49 ch3. Channel0 large maybe not many. Agent position could be near bottom-right? If the agent is typically at bottom-right? That said though, I expect a sufficiently experienced human being armed with a notepad and a pencil could get there with enough effort. It's a cool paper, but some of the wider commentary I've seen around it does not feel justified. I'm not ready to declare that the age of source code is over and our future involves incomprehensible machines editing their own model weights in incomprehensible ways. # RustXNG [日本語](README.ja.md) · [한국어](README.ko.md) RustXNG is a self-hosted metasearch engine written in Rust, based on [SearXNG](https://github.com/searxng/searxng). It combines results from external search providers and can fetch page text for AI agents through a JSON API or MCP. RustXNG does not maintain a web-scale search index. You can add a local index of selected sites with `rustxng-index` and import Wikipedia dumps separately. ## Quick start Install from the [releases page](https://github.com/sahenjp/RustXNG/releases) or with Cargo. Release binaries are available for Linux, macOS and Windows; check the matching asset and its SHA-256 sidecar before running it. <!-- x-release-please-start-version --> ```bash cargo install --git https://github.com/sahenjp/RustXNG.git --tag v0.30.0 --locked ``` <!-- x-release-please-end --> Rust 1.88 or newer and a C build toolchain are required for source installation. The [agent setup guide](docs/AGENT-SETUP.md) covers release binaries, verification, platform requirements and service reuse. Start a local server: ```bash rustxng --bind 127.0.0.1 --port 29483 ``` Search from another terminal: ```bash curl --fail --get 'http://127.0.0.1:29483/search' \ --data-urlencode 'q=tokio runtime documentation' \ --data 'format=json' --data 'max_results=5' ``` Results contain a title, URL, snippet and source metadata. For automated clients that need errors for unknown engine names, add `strict_engines=1` (the default preserves SearXNG-compatible fallback behavior). Useful optional parameters include `language=ja`, `engines=wikipedia`, `include_domains=docs.rs`, `exclude_domains=example.com`, `time_range=day`, and `include_raw_content=1`. Time filtering depends on provider support. The web interface is at <http://127.0.0.1:29483/>. The search endpoint also supports CSV, RSS and HTML output. ## Use from an AI agent Start the built-in MCP server: ```bash rustxng mcp ``` MCP exposes two read-only tools: - `search` returns up to 10 ranked results. # sandbox MicroVM sandboxes for AI agents, built on [cocoon](https://github.com/cocoonstack/cocoon): a fast-boot guest stack, an in-guest product daemon, a per-node control plane with warm pools, and SDKs for Go and Python. Warm claims are sub-millisecond; a pool miss clones from a golden snapshot in tens of milliseconds; cold boot is ~0.2–0.4 s on bare metal. **Documentation: [cocoonstack.github.io/sandbox](https://cocoonstack.github.io/sandbox/)** (source in [`docs/`](docs/)). ## Architecture ``` SDK (Go/Python) sandboxd (per node) guest microVM client.New/new ─ HTTP ─► claim: warm pool / golden clone Cloud Hypervisor exec/files/… ─ HTTP upgrade (kept) ─► byte relay ─ vsock ─► silkd :2048 memberlist mesh: warm-count gossip, MOVED-style redirect to the owning node ``` Cloud Hypervisor serves both network lanes. `net=none` has no NIC and uses vsock-only I/O (hardened default); `net=egress` attaches a bridge/CNI NIC. ## Quick start On a Linux node with KVM, [cocoon](https://github.com/cocoonstack/cocoon) v0.6.9 or newer, Cloud Hypervisor and `jq`, as root, from a checkout with Go installed. Not on a node that already runs sandboxd on the same cocoon root: at start sandboxd removes every `sbx-` VM it does not own. ```bash make sandboxd cocoon image pull ghcr.io/cocoonstack/sandbox/rt:24.04 cat >config.json <<'EOF' { "listen": "127.0.0.1:7777", "api_token": "change-me", "pools": [ {"template": "ghcr.io/cocoonstack/sandbox/rt:24.04", "net": "none", "size": "small", "warm": 2} ] } EOF dist/sandboxd -config config.json & # Wait for the golden snapshot and the warm pool. until curl -sf -H 'Authorization: Bearer change-me' http://127.0.0.1:7777/v1/info | jq -e '(.pools | length) > 0 and all(.pools[]; .golden and .warm >= .target)' >/dev/null; do sleep 1; done # Claim, exec and release three times; prints each latency. (cd e2e && GOWORK=off go run ./cmd/demo -addr 127.0.0.1:7777 -token change-me \ -template ghcr.io/cocoonstack/sandbox/rt:24.04) ``` A stopped sandboxd leaves its VMs for the next start. To remove them: ```bash kill %1 cocoon vm list --format json | jq -r '.[].config.name | select(startswith("sbx-"))' | while read -r vm; do cocoon vm stop --force "$vm"; cocoon vm rm --force "$vm"; done ``` `demo` is a small program over the [Go SDK](docs/sdk.md); the [Python SDK](docs/sdk-python.md) has the same calls. [Deploying sandboxd](docs/deploy.md) covers release

# pi-goal-list-loop-audit

> **Give Pi an outcome—not another prompt to stop halfway through.** GLLA turns substantial work into a durable, supervised process: agree on the finish line, keep working across turns, recover interruptions, and check the result before calling it complete. ```bash pi install npm:pi-goal-list-loop-audit ``` Then, in Pi: ```text /goal plan Make this project's first-run experience ready for new users ``` Review the proposed objective and acceptance criteria, confirm them, and let Pi work. Use `/glla status` to see what it is doing and what needs your attention. **Waiting** yields to named background work while supervision remains active; **paused** freezes automatic continuation. See [waiting and recovery](docs/RECOVERY.md#waiting-is-not-paused). Keep `pi-agent-core`, `pi-ai`, `pi-coding-agent` and `pi-tui` on the same version. See [compatibility](docs/COMPATIBILITY.md) for what is tested versus merely covered by the range. - **Node 22.19 or newer.** Upgrading Pi inside that range needs no GLLA change; GLLA no longer declares an upper bound that stops at the 0.x line. ## About GLLA Coding agents are good at taking the next step. # Phantom **Your agent can call the API. The key stays in a local vault.** Phantom replaces managed secrets in `.env` with `phm_` placeholders. Agents and apps read those placeholders. A proxy on `127.0.0.1` adds the vault value only to the auth header of a matched route.
